name: Volga Bulgaria
summary: A Turkic state on the middle Volga that converted to Islam in 922 and grew rich from the fur trade, until the Mongols conquered it.

knownFor.label: Ibn Fadlan’s journey
knownFor.note: An Abbasid envoy who described the Volga Bulgars.

knownFor.label: Bolghar
knownFor.note: Ruined city, a World Heritage Site.

knownFor.label: Fur trade
knownFor.note: Furs from the north sold south.

location.value: Around the confluence of the Volga and Kama rivers in European Russia; the capital Bolghar lay about 160 km south of modern Kazan.

terrain.value: Forest-steppe with rich black soils, broad river valleys and forests to the north.

climate.value: Continental: long, cold winters with frozen rivers, and warm summers good for grain.

resources.value: Furs from the northern forests, fertile soil for grain, honey and wax, fish, and control of river trade.

disasters.value: Not recorded in detail; poor harvests and famine are mentioned in neighbouring Rus’ chronicles.

population.value: No figure is given. It was a multi-ethnic state (Bulgars, Finno-Ugrians, Varangians, East Slavs and Turkic groups), and about two-thirds of the population was destroyed after the Mongol conquest.

urbanisation.value: Bolghar, Bilär and Suvar were large walled towns; Bilär may have been one of the biggest towns in Eastern Europe.

disease.value: Not recorded in detail; epidemics probably spread along the busy river trade routes.

migration.value: Bulgars moved north from the Black Sea steppe (7th century).

economicBase.value: Before the Crusades it controlled much of the trade between Europe and Asia; furs and slaves were the main goods, exchanged for Arab silver dirhams and silk.

tradeRoutes.value: Controlled much of the Volga trade between Europe and Asia, reaching Norse and northern peoples, Baghdad, Constantinople and China; slaves and furs were traded for Arab silver dirhams.

wealth.value: A rich trading centre whose merchants handled furs and silver dirhams from Central Asia.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver coins copying Samanid dirhams from the 900s; rulers taxed traders, often a tenth of their goods.

inequality.value: Not well recorded; rulers and merchants grew rich from trade.

governmentType.value: The infobox gives a monarchy (the state is sometimes called the Volga Bulgar Emirate); Ibn Fadlan called the ruler “King of the Saqaliba”. The title “khan” is not mentioned in the part of the page read.

keyRulers.value: Kotrag is remembered as the founder; Almış sent an envoy to the Caliph in 921 and the state adopted Islam in 922.

succession.value: Hereditary within the ruling family, though records are few.

institutions.value: Islamic law and judges, the emir’s court, and tax collectors at river trading posts.

stability.value: Stable trading state for about three centuries.

eliteConflict.value: Not well recorded; local nobles and towns may have competed for power.

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry, archers and fortified towns with earth ramparts and wooden walls.

majorWars.value: Rus’ raids devastated the country in the 11th century; in 1220 Yuri II of Vladimir captured Ustiug and besieged Aşlı; a Mongol advance guard was beaten at Samara Bend in 1223; the Mongols returned in 1236 and subjugated the country within five years. The entry’s 985 and 1164 are not on the page.

territoryChange.value: Conquered by the Mongols, who destroyed Bilär in 1236.

alliancesRivals.value: Ties to the Abbasid Caliphate after 922; rivals of the Khazars and Rus’ princes; trading partners of Central Asia.

inventions.value: Not recorded; skilled in metalwork and leather.

scienceEducation.value: Islamic schools and scholars; Ibn Fadlan’s 922 visit describes the court, and some local scholars wrote in Arabic.

openness.value: Open to trade with Rus’, Scandinavians, Central Asians and Baghdad, as described by Ibn Fadlan.

communicationTransport.value: River boats on the Volga and Kama, and overland caravans to Central Asia.

religion.value: Adopted Islam as the state religion in 922 after Almış sent an ambassador to the Caliph in 921, 66 years before Kievan Rus’ was Christianised.

languageWriting.value: Bulgar Turkic, related to modern Chuvash, written in Arabic script; Arabic for religion and learning.

artsArchitecture.value: Mosques, bathhouses and mausoleums of brick and stone at Bilär and Bolghar; skilled metal, leather and pottery work.

socialStructure.value: Not recorded in detail; emir, nobles, merchants, farmers.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared Muslim Bulgar identity among the townspeople, distinct from nearby Rus’ and forest peoples.

dailyLife.value: Wooden and brick houses; bread, meat, fish.

neighbours.value: The Khazars to the south, the Rus’ to the west, Finno-Ugric forest peoples to the north, and Kipchak nomads; later the Mongols.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Islam north into the forest zone; its people later passed Islam to the Volga Tatars.

colonisation.value: None; it did not found colonies, though it collected tribute from forest peoples to the north.

riseSignals.value: Old Great Bulgaria was founded about 630 and destroyed by the Khazars in 668; the Bulgars reached the Volga in the eighth century and were dominant there by the end of the ninth. The capital was Bolghar, 160 km south of modern Kazan.

peakPeriod.value: The 10th–12th centuries, when its towns, trade and coinage flourished.

declineSignals.value: The Mongol invasion destroyed its towns (1236), after an earlier Mongol defeat about 1223.

outcome.value: The Mongols returned in 1236 and subjugated the country within five years (the infobox says the 1240s); it became vassal principalities of the Golden Horde, and the Khanate of Kazan was the most important by the 1430s.
